name: Nyambo
catalog_quote: If a root bears a stress, that stress will be realized on the initial syllable of the root. ... There is a language-specific prohibition in Kinyambo against a prominence in phrase-final position.
sweep_summary: Nyambo (nyam1277) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Bickmore 1989. All four sweep items are Bickmore or Bickmore-derived. (1) Bickmore 1989, pp.47-53 re-read and pp.50/53 checked against page images) confirms: roots are stressed or stressless, stress is realized root-initially as H, phrase-final prominence is banned, nine penult exceptions are loans/reduplications. (2) Bickmore 1992 (Phonology 9) remains paywalled (Crossref/OpenAlex/Unpaywall/S2 closed, no author copy on his Wayback-archived UAlbany pages); only the Cambridge 'Extract' (closing paragraph) is open and it asserts multiple phonemic stress levels, consistent with the lexical coding, silent on placement; priority medium. (3) Philippson 1991 thesis (author PDF already held under bemb1257; Nyambo passages extracted to is new to the per-language bibliography: p.500 classifies Nyambo as 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H' with 'H s'associe à la syllabe marquée' and a pre-pausal penult vs contextual final alternation; p.413/487 place it among Rutara languages that reduced tone to accent via Meeussen's rule; second-hand (from Bickmore 1988) and confirms. (4) Bickmore 1990 (Inkelas & Zec volume) is a phrasal-phonology chapter, print-only (Google Books partial preview blocked, no archive.org/HathiTrust copy); priority low. Best statement read remains the catalog's own deciding source (Bickmore 1989 p.50/53); no supersession. discovery used Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, archive.org, the Google Books feed and Wayback. updated at

new_statements.quote: If a root bears a stress, that stress will be realized on the initial syllable of the root. With the exception of monosyllabic roots and the word a-má-iso 'eyes' (which cases will be discussed below), all the forms in Table I conform to this statement. There are, however, some surface exceptions to this generalization. There are nine cases known to me (out of approximately 380 nouns in my data base) in which a High tone is born by a non-initial mora in a noun root. [...] [p.53] I will assume that monosyllabic roots are like other roots in that some may be stressed and some stressless. There is a language-specific prohibition in Kinyambo against a prominence in phrase-final position.
new_statements.citation: Bickmore, Lee Stephen. 1989. Kinyambo Prosody. PhD dissertation, UCLA, printed p.50 sec.3.3 and p.53 sec.3.5
new_statements.locator: printed p.50 sec.3.3 'The position of underlying prominence' (PDF 68); printed p.53 sec.3.5 (PDF 71)
new_statements.reading: Stress in Kinyambo is a lexical property of roots (some roots stressed, some stressless; Table I p.47 has All-Low nouns at every length), and when a root is stressed the stress is realized on the root-initial syllable, surfacing as a High (or Falling) tone; a ban on phrase-final prominence shifts a monosyllabic root's stress leftward onto the prefix, and nine penult-stressed nouns are Swahili loans or reduplications. Philippson 1991 (p.500, second-hand from Bickmore 1988) independently classifies Nyambo as an accentual language whose H docks on the lexically marked syllable. This supports the catalog's 'lexical' coding exactly; nothing new read in this sweep supersedes it.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction to the coding. One small overstatement in the reader's gloss: the nine penult-H nouns (p.50 ex. 1) are not all "Swahili loans or reduplications" — Bickmore sorts them as three loans (e-barúa, e-zawáadi, e-papái), two or three reduplications (o-ru-huguhúgu, e-ki-zuunguzúungu, possibly e-ki-goongóro), two derived nominalisations (e-ch-akúrya, o-mu-tamíire) and one unexplained (e-ñañíiñi 'star', pp.51-52); fn.4 p.50 puts the exception count at twelve of 620 stems. This does not change the bearing.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every piece of the deciding text (Bickmore 1989:48, 50, 51, 53) is present verbatim in the held scan at the stated sections/pages (PDF = printed + 18), confirmed from the on-disk scanned of those pages; Table I p.47 shows All-Low nouns at all lengths and p.53 states roots may be 'stressed' or 'stressless', which is exactly the basis for coding prominence as a lexical property with root-initial realization. (2) Deciding source: a 229-pp UCLA phonology dissertation (1989) wholly on Kinyambo prosody, fieldwork-based, top of Glottolog's list; its 1992 Phonology article is the same analysis. Nothing later addresses word prominence: France 2021 (fetched sources now, open AJOL) is segmental and silent; Hubbard is duration phonetics; Katamba 1991/Odden 1995 are survey chapters.

sources.quote: p.500: "Nyambo : 1. : oui (2) 3. : langue accentuelle à mélodie H 4. : 2 5. : -cv(:)cv et -c&v(:)cv•/-cv(:)c&v.... 6? 7. : ? 8. : H s'associe à la syllabe marquée 9. : H associé à la pénultième devant pause s'associe à la finale en contexte 10. : ?" p.413: "Le nyambo aurait confondu BH, HB et HH dans un schème unique réalisé HB devant pause et BH en contexte." p.487: "Les langues lacustres ont, pour la plupart abouti au même point, sous l'influence de la règle de Meeussen : c'est le cas du nyankore, du haya et du nyambo, ainsi que du ganda." [EN: p.500: 'Nyambo: accentual language with H melody; 2 [prosodic types in disyllabic themes]; H associates to the marked syllable; H associated with the penult before pause associates to the final syllable in context.' p.413: 'Nyambo appears to have merged BH, HB and HH into a single scheme realized HB before pause and BH in context.' p.487: 'Most of the Lacustrine languages have reached the same point [stage III, reduction of the tone system to an accentual system] under the influence of Meeussen's rule: nyankore, haya and nyambo, and also ganda.']
sources.locator: p.500 (Appendix typological sheet 'Nyambo'); p.413 (ch.6 summary); p.487 (ch.6 sec.3.6.1); p.78 Tableau II; p.188; p.517 (bibliography for Nyambo = Bickmore 1988 ACAL paper only)
sources.note: Second-hand comparative typology (his only Nyambo source is Bickmore's 1988 ACAL handout). Classifies Nyambo as an accentual language with an H melody in which H docks on the lexically marked syllable, with two prosodic classes of disyllabic themes (marked vs unmarked: -cv(:)cv vs -cv́(:)cv before pause / -cv(:)cv́ in context), the pre-pausal penult vs contextual final alternation matching Bickmore's phrase-final prohibition and the omugóre/omugoré waange pair. Does not itself state root-initial placement.
